question: Can the most common machine-learning losses be organized into a single task-and-mechanism taxonomy that reliably guides loss selection?

key_findings.claim: The paper assembles a broad pedagogical catalogue of 43 named objectives across regression, classification, generative modeling, ranking, and energy-based modeling, with a second axis of error-, probabilistic-, and margin-based strategy.
key_findings.evidence: The main taxonomy connects five task regions, three strategy regions, and weight-based regularization. The text gives formulas, brief use cases, advantages, drawbacks, and labels for continuity, differentiability, Lipschitz continuity, convexity, or strict convexity. Coverage extends from MAE/MSE and cross-entropy through VAE/GAN/diffusion objectives, metric learning, LambdaLoss, and classical EBM losses.

key_findings.claim: This is a narrative catalogue rather than a reproducible survey, so its claims of comprehensiveness, wide use, and optimal application contexts cannot be audited from the paper.
key_findings.evidence: There is no search query, database list, date range, screening flow, inclusion/exclusion rule, citation threshold, duplicate policy, quality appraisal, or extraction protocol. The authors state that they selected 43 of the most widely used losses, but provide neither usage measurements nor a comparison table showing why excluded families fall outside scope. The conclusion repeats that the taxonomy can identify the most suitable loss without any validation study.

anchors.section: 2 Definition of our loss function taxonomy

key_findings.claim: The mathematical-property badges are not consistently defined with respect to predictions, logits, distributions, or model parameters, and several badges are false under ordinary interpretations.
key_findings.evidence: Convexity and Lipschitz continuity depend on the argument and domain. The survey labels cross-entropy and language-model losses convex while acknowledging that composition with a neural model is nonconvex; labels VAE/CVAE objectives Lipschitz without bounding the encoder/decoder; calls VQ-VAE 'continuous overall' despite its discrete argmin quantizer; and labels cosine loss Lipschitz/differentiable although it is undefined at zero. It also asserts that strict convexity gives an everywhere positive-definite Hessian, invertibility, and a closed-form solution, none of which follows in general.

key_findings.claim: The classification chapter contains source-rendered equations that do not define the named losses.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 23 calls a branch-reversed function Ramp loss: it returns hinge when the signed margin is at most 1 and returns 1 above 1, jumping from 0 to 1 at the boundary despite being labeled continuous and convex. Equation 24 defines one-minus-cosine, whose range is [0,2], while the text says [-1,1]. Equation 35 averages negative log probability over every class without a one-hot target; under the simplex constraint it is minimized by a uniform prediction rather than the correct class. Equations 30-32 also equate a sum of log-likelihoods to a scaled product, an algebraically invalid step.

anchors.section: 5.2.6 Ramp loss and 5.2.7 Cosine Similarity loss

key_findings.claim: The generative-model coverage omits constraints or misstates computation in ways that change the objectives' meaning.
key_findings.evidence: The WGAN section gives critic and generator scores but omits the essential 1-Lipschitz critic constraint; without it the Kantorovich-dual maximization is unbounded and is not the Wasserstein distance. The score-based section says training requires higher-order derivatives of the score, although denoising score matching ordinarily backpropagates through a network that directly predicts the score/noise. Several global continuity/Lipschitz labels are inherited from component losses even though the parameterized neural objectives need not have those properties.

key_findings.claim: The ranking chapter's two most modern formulas are not normalized or oriented as the named methods require.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 63 omits the positive pair from the NT-Xent denominator, leaving only N negatives; the resulting ratio can exceed one and its negative log can be negative, so it is not a cross-entropy probability. Equation 64 calls |Delta NDCG| times sigmoid(f_i-f_j) LambdaLoss and proposes minimizing it without a relevance-order sign or negative log; for y_i greater than y_j, minimization pushes f_i-f_j negative. This is not the standard LambdaRank/LambdaLoss gradient or pairwise logistic objective, and the ranking-dependent Delta NDCG term also conflicts with the blanket differentiability claim.

key_findings.claim: The energy-based negative log-likelihood has the opposite partition-function sign from the paper's own Boltzmann definition.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 67 defines p_theta(x) proportional to exp(-E_theta(x)). Its negative log-likelihood must therefore contain E plus log integral exp(-E), with the same negative exponent. Equation 72 instead uses exp(+beta E) while retaining +E/beta scaling. This is not shift-invariant and can be driven by globally lowering energies, so it is not the stated EBM NLL and does not reduce to the claimed perceptron objective as written.

key_findings.claim: The survey offers no empirical or formal evaluation of its taxonomy, equations, property labels, or selection advice.
key_findings.evidence: There are no experiments, worked loss-selection case studies, inter-rater agreement checks, implementation tests, symbolic checks, benchmark comparisons, or sensitivity analyses. Figures 1-6 are conceptual relationship diagrams only. Consequently, the paper cannot demonstrate that its taxonomy helps users choose better objectives or that its formulas reproduce canonical implementations.

method.core_idea: Organize common losses first by application family and then by whether their construction is primarily error-, probability-, or margin-based, while annotating optimization properties and practical tradeoffs.
method.mechanism: The paper begins with generic empirical-risk notation and regularization, introduces property badges and optimizer summaries, then walks through formulas and prose descriptions for each loss family. Six diagrams connect related objectives and the bibliography points to original or representative applications.
assumptions: Forty-three author-selected losses are representative of the most widely used machine-learning objectives.
Task and underlying mathematical strategy provide sufficient axes for practical selection.
Properties such as convexity, differentiability, and Lipschitz continuity can be attached to a named loss without consistently specifying its argument, parameterization, or domain.
Short qualitative descriptions can characterize advantages, limitations, and optimal application contexts without comparative experiments.
Losses, divergences, regularizers, composite training objectives, and model-family objectives can be placed in one diagram at comparable granularity.

techniques.role: Partition objectives into regression, classification, generative, ranking, and energy-based uses.
Overlay error-based, probabilistic, and margin-based construction families.
Annotate sections with continuity, differentiability, Lipschitz, convexity, and strict-convexity labels.
Provide a compact mathematical definition and narrative tradeoff summary for each named loss.
Use six figures to connect base losses, regularized variants, and application-specific extensions.

evaluations.setting: Narrative coverage of 43 author-selected losses and several regularizers across five task families.
evaluations.metric: Qualitative breadth, mathematical formula, property badges, use cases, advantages, and limitations.
evaluations.result: The catalogue is broad and easy to browse, but no systematic-review statistic, correctness audit, or user outcome is reported.
evaluations.baseline: Earlier general and application-specific loss surveys are cited but not compared by a reproducible coverage matrix.

limitations: No reproducible literature-search or study-selection protocol supports the coverage claims.

The taxonomy is neither mutually exclusive nor exhaustive: many objectives are simultaneously error-, probabilistic-, and margin-related, while calibration, robustness, proper scoring rules, structured prediction, optimal transport, survival, causal, and reinforcement-learning objectives receive little or no treatment.
Properties are not parameterization-invariant and the paper rarely states the variable and domain with respect to which a badge applies.
No code accompanies the formula catalogue, despite errors that simple numerical property tests would catch.
No experiments establish which loss is preferable under noise, imbalance, distribution shift, calibration, computational budget, or target-metric mismatch.

The revised 2024 coverage of LLMs and diffusion remains introductory and omits preference optimization, sequence-level risk, flow matching, consistency objectives, and modern multimodal contrastive variants.
failure_modes: Implementing Equation 23 produces a discontinuous reverse truncation rather than ramp loss.
Implementing Equation 35 trains multiclass predictions toward uniformity because target labels are absent.
Implementing Equation 63 can yield negative 'NT-Xent' values because the positive is absent from the normalizer.
Implementing Equation 64 with gradient descent reverses a correctly ordered document pair under the stated orientation.
Implementing Equation 72 does not define the likelihood corresponding to Equation 67 and is unbounded under energy shifts.
Treating component-level convexity or differentiability as a property of a neural training problem can lead to invalid optimizer guarantees.
reusable_insights: A loss atlas should make the optimized variable, prediction domain, reduction convention, and model composition explicit for every property claim.
Every catalogue formula can be paired with executable reference code and property-based tests for symmetry, range, boundary continuity, shift invariance, and known special cases.
Practical selection needs axes beyond task: noise model, target metric, calibration, imbalance, tail risk, optimization geometry, compute, and robustness to shift.
A graph representation is useful when edges have typed semantics such as limit, regularized variant, surrogate, probabilistic derivation, or task specialization.
Loss choice can be treated as a bilevel or evolutionary search problem, but search results require transfer and leakage controls.
open_questions: Can a versioned, executable loss ontology automatically verify formulas against canonical implementations and published limiting cases?
Which loss properties measured in prediction space actually predict convergence and generalization after composition with modern neural architectures?
Can loss recommendations be validated prospectively across datasets using nested selection rather than post-hoc task anecdotes?
How should automated loss search trade validation performance against calibration, robustness, interpretability, and transfer to new architectures?
What minimal set of typed relations makes a large interactive loss graph more useful than a flat task taxonomy?

competitive_landscape.title: Loss Functions and Metrics in Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: A direct broad successor reference covering common deep-learning losses and evaluation metrics across regression, classification, computer vision, and NLP.
competitive_landscape.difference: It explicitly distinguishes training losses from performance metrics and broadens task-level metric coverage; the present survey has a more compact relationship taxonomy and an energy-based chapter but no metric ontology.

competitive_landscape.title: Loss Functions in Deep Learning: A Comprehensive Review
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later general review spanning foundational, adversarial, diffusion, multimodal, tabular, and time-series objectives with historical and computational perspectives.
competitive_landscape.difference: It is more current and application-oriented and adds future directions around adaptive and robust objectives; the 2023 survey's main differentiator remains its single cross-task graph, not coverage or empirical validation.

competitive_landscape.title: A survey of loss functions for semantic segmentation
competitive_landscape.relationship: A narrower loss survey that links segmentation objectives to imbalance regimes and evaluates a proposed log-cosh Dice loss on a public dataset.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its scope is much smaller, but it supplies executable code and an empirical comparison; the present paper trades that testability for breadth and therefore cannot substantiate its selection guidance.

competitive_landscape.title: AM-LFS: AutoML for Loss Function Search
competitive_landscape.relationship: Replaces manual selection with a bilevel REINFORCE search over a unified parameterized family of visual-recognition losses.
competitive_landscape.difference: AM-LFS operationalizes 'which loss?' against validation reward and reports transfer experiments, whereas the survey offers static qualitative recommendations; its search space is task-specific and can overfit validation choices.

competitive_landscape.title: AutoLoss-Zero: Searching Loss Functions From Scratch for Generic Tasks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Uses evolutionary search over primitive computational graphs with rejection and gradient-equivalence checks to discover objectives for multiple task metrics.
competitive_landscape.difference: It explores objective space beyond named handcrafted losses and directly optimizes downstream metrics; the survey's taxonomy could seed such a search, but it does not address search cost, selection bias, or transfer.

competitive_landscape.title: The Central Role of the Loss Function in Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: A theory-focused survey and analysis showing how regression and distributional losses change first- and second-order sample-efficiency bounds in decision making.
competitive_landscape.difference: It provides task-specific theorems that connect loss choice to statistical efficiency, a major family absent from the present taxonomy; its scope is RL/cost-sensitive learning rather than a general formula handbook.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a comprehensive 43-loss reference and a novel, intuitive taxonomy that clarifies foundations, properties, relationships, and optimal application contexts.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Its main distinctive artifact is a single visual graph crossing five application areas with three construction strategies, supported by a long formula-and-prose catalogue that includes both classical statistics and recent generative modeling.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The breadth and compact diagrams make it a useful list of search terms, but prior general and domain surveys already offered loss catalogues, and later surveys cover modern deep-learning uses more fully. The purported guidance is not evaluated, selection is not systematic, property badges are ill-posed, and multiple central formulas are mathematically wrong in the rendered source. Its safest role is orientation, not an implementation reference or authoritative taxonomy.

reviewer_notes: Read all 55 PDF pages: pages 1-42 contain the complete survey and conclusion, pages 42-55 the full bibliography, and page 55 was rendered directly because the extraction index marks it missing; it contains only the end of reference 160 and the page number. All six taxonomy/application diagrams and the rendered equations on pages 13, 18-20, 36-37, and 40 were visually inspected. The ramp, categorical-cross-entropy, NT-Xent, LambdaLoss, and EBM-NLL errors are present in the pinned PDF and are not extraction artifacts. Six direct primary competitors or alternative approaches were checked on official arXiv/CVF records through 2026-08-23. No symbolic test suite or implementation rerun was performed.
